reason: Supra-axillary (arising above the axil) is a kind of extra-axillary (arising outside the axil), so the mapping is true, only less specific. With 7 statements a rule is enough. 'Above' is a finer position that has no term.

Ascending (PATO:0104355) covers parts directed obliquely upward. 'Arcuately' only says how the curve runs and can be dropped, as other accepted rules do (e.g. 'longitudinally fissured' -> fissured). The mapping is true.

In the floras 'columellate' describes pollen exine (rod-like columellae) and lichen apothecia. PO_0025230 columella covers fruit and moss-capsule columellae, which are different structures, and no PO class fits the other senses.

The definition of FLOPO:0991203 alveolate (close-set angular pits like a honeycomb) already implies a network of walls between the pits. 'Reticulate' only names those walls, so nothing important is lost.

Glossaries give 'excised' as 'with a notch cut out'. On an apex, tip or edge that is PATO:0002234 emarginate ('having a notched tip or edge'). On other parts the word can mean 'cut away' more generally.

A plain pato rule puts the quality on the part named in the sentence, so 'leaves obscurely nerved' would give 'leaf inconspicuous', which is false. The rule kind cannot set the veins (PO:0005020) as the part. 'Obscure' (C174) already covers 'obscure veins', where the veins are named.
Flask-shaped (FLOPO:0991183) needs a body swollen below plus a neck. 'Narrow-necked' states only the neck, and the rule's own note found a case that does not fit. Too doubtful for 4 statements.

In 'leaf base narrowed and petiolelike', the taper comes from 'narrowed'. 'Petiolelike' alone means stalk-like (e.g. a pseudopetiole or claw), not 'tapering to a slender point' as PATO:0001982 attenuate is defined.
Fragile fits only 'readily tearing'. The bare word also describes how spathes or sheaths split or open (dehiscence), so the rule is ambiguous.

A knob-shaped stigma or hair tip is head-shaped (FLOPO:0991097: abruptly enlarged at the tip into a rounded head; the term already applies to stigma and trichome). On other parts a knob can be a swelling anywhere.
Root nodule present (PO_0003023) is right only for roots and plants. Nodules on leaves (bacterial leaf nodules) are not root nodules. The rule's own note says it is for roots only.

The rule already applies only to whole plants. Virgate (FLOPO:0991038) lists 'broom-like' as a related synonym. A broom-like shrub (e.g. Retama, Cytisus) is one with many slender, straight, erect twigs, which is the virgate habit.

It negates constricted. For an aroid spathe, constriction would be in the middle (between tube and blade), so 'not constricted' says the same thing. The rule's note says the region (centrally) is handled separately.

Glossaries give 'pilulose' as minutely pilose (very small, fine hairs), which falls under puberulous (FLOPO:0991049: very short, fine, soft hairs). It is not 'pilular' (ball-shaped). With 66 statements, the hair sense is the one the floras use.

This matches the accepted rules R0450, R0606 and R0640, which map 'not keeled', 'ecarinate' and 'without keel' to 'not keel-shaped'. In glumes, lemmas and fruits the keel is a ridge, not a separate part. PO_0025327 keel is the pea-family petal keel, so an absence rule would use the wrong class.
Same as R0830 and R0606 (ecarinate): keelless means not carinate. PO keel is the pea-family petal keel and cannot be used here.

In the French floras, 'rampant(e)' on axes and plants means creeping (FLOPO:0991009, synonym repent). The English sense 'growing vigorously' and use on other parts should not get the rule. These parts match the creeping term's own part list.
Delimited means marked off or bounded, often by different cells (e.g. moss alar cells). It is not visibility of the part. The bare key would also fire inside 'poorly delimited'.

Nigrescent means blackish or turning black. A tint near black is still black (PATO:0000317), and the 'when dry' and stage readings are handled by the existing pattern for specimen condition (docs/odp/06-specimen-condition.md) and by stage words.

'Sheathed' usually means enclosed by a sheath (passive), while FLOPO:0991105 sheathing means the part itself wraps the axis. 'Not sheathed' (e.g. spines 'neither sheathed nor barbed') does not clearly negate sheathing.

Shreddy bark peeling in strips fits exfoliating (FLOPO:0991021), which is defined for bark and the axes that carry it. On other parts (e.g. fibrous leaf sheaths) 'shreddy' is fibrous tearing, not exfoliation.
Multicipital (many-headed) is branching of a caudex, rootstock or taproot crown into several heads. Branched (PATO:0000402) is true for those parts only.
On margins, walls and blades 'thinned' (French 'aminci') means thinner, i.e. decreased thickness. On other parts (e.g. a thinned indumentum) it can mean less dense.

The word is said of the plant, and a pato rule cannot move the quality to the stem. The result would be 'whole plant decreased strength', which is wrong. It needs a rule kind or pattern that sets stem (PO_0009047) as the part.
Radiate (FLOPO:0991194) is defined for a capitulum with ray flowers. Also, 'daisy-like flowers' appears in non-composites (e.g. Aizoaceae), where radiate is false, so 'flower' is left out.
'Nervation pennée' and pennate blades or leaflets are pinnately veined (FLOPO:0991201). For a whole leaf, 'pennate' can mean pinnate with leaflets, so leaf is left out.

Multiveined implies veined, and this matches the accepted rules C211 and C212 ('veined', 'nerved' -> vascular bundle present). The statement is true. 'Many' is not a number the counting rules can take, so leaving it out loses detail without making it false.
An elongate rhomb is still rhomboid (PATO:0001938). 'Long' is a degree within the shape, handled as in 'depressed-globose'. The mapping is true for the moss leaf cells it describes.
For underground organs, deep-seated means well below the soil surface, which is subterranean (FLOPO:0991035). Glands, veins or cells can also be deep-seated (sunken), and that is not this position.
'Graceful' describes how a part looks. PATO slender lists 'gracile' only as a related synonym, and for whole plants the word is vague. Too doubtful for a rule.
